final_writeup:
No full proof or planar counterexample was obtained. The principal positive result is stronger with respect to balance weights but restricted structurally: every vertex-weighted graph of treewidth at most three has a half-balanced separator contained in two geodesics of the original graph. More generally, the conclusion follows from any tree decomposition whose bags are two-geodesic-coverable. Thus a planar counterexample must have treewidth at least four, at least nine vertices, and no half-balanced separator of order at most four.

Further sufficient conditions cover balanced five-vertex separators containing an induced three-vertex path, balanced isometric cycles of arbitrary length, all balanced 5-cycles in planar graphs, and balanced induced cycles of length six.

Two limitations are proved explicitly. First, one cannot obtain the desired result merely by discarding one member of a known three-geodesic separator: an infinite planar family has three specified geodesics whose union balances, while none of their pairwise unions does. Second, one geodesic is genuinely insufficient: the icosahedral graph has no half-balanced geodesic, although two explicit geodesics do balance it. The global two-geodesic planar question remains unresolved by these arguments.

results.claim: It suffices to treat connected nonempty graphs.
results.proof_sketch: If every component of G already has order at most n/2, deleting any path vertices preserves this. Otherwise there is a unique component H of order greater than n/2. A separator supplied inside H leaves components of H of order at most |H|/2<=n/2, while every other component of G has order at most n-|H|<n/2. Distances between vertices of H are unchanged because H is a connected component, so H-geodesics are G-geodesics.

results.claim: Balancedness is monotone under enlarging the deleted set.
results.proof_sketch: If X is half-balanced and X is contained in Y, every component of G-Y is a connected subgraph of a component of G-X. Its order (or nonnegative vertex weight) therefore cannot be larger.

results.claim: In a connected graph, every set X of at most four vertices is contained in the union of two geodesics.
results.proof_sketch: For four vertices, partition X into two pairs and take a shortest path joining each pair. For three vertices, join two by a shortest path and use a one-vertex path for the third (or join it to either of the first two). The cases of one or two vertices are immediate. Extra internal vertices on the chosen paths cause no difficulty.

results.claim: Any graph having a half-balanced vertex separator of order at most four satisfies the two-geodesic conclusion; the same statement holds for arbitrary nonnegative vertex weights.
results.proof_sketch: After the connected reduction, cover the separator by two geodesics using the preceding claim. Their union is a superset of the original separator, so monotonicity preserves half-balance.

results.claim: Every nonnegatively weighted finite tree has a centroid node whose deletion leaves tree components of weight at most half the total.
results.proof_sketch: For each tree edge, direct it toward a side having weight greater than half, if such a side exists. Starting anywhere and following directed edges cannot revisit a node and hence terminates. At the terminal node no incident side has weight greater than half.

results.claim: Every vertex-weighted graph tree decomposition has a half-balanced bag.
results.proof_sketch: Recall that bags containing any fixed vertex form a connected subtree and every graph edge has both endpoints in some bag. Assign each graph vertex and its weight to one bag containing it, and choose a centroid t of the resulting weighted decomposition tree. Let K be a component of G-B_t. Each vertex v of K has a bag-subtree avoiding t. Bag-subtrees of adjacent vertices intersect, so connectivity of K puts all these subtrees in one component R of T-t. The assigned bag of every v in K lies in R; hence w(K) is at most the assigned weight of R, which is at most half the total.

results.claim: If a connected graph has a tree decomposition in which every bag is contained in the union of two geodesics of the original graph, then those geodesics yield a half-balanced separator for every nonnegative vertex weighting.
results.proof_sketch: Choose the half-balanced bag supplied by the preceding claim and then choose its two-geodesic cover. The cover may delete additional vertices, but balancedness is monotone.

results.claim: Every graph of treewidth at most three satisfies the target, even with arbitrary nonnegative vertex weights; planarity is unnecessary.
results.proof_sketch: Treewidth at most three means that a tree decomposition exists with at most four vertices in each bag. By the four-vertex covering claim, every such bag is contained in two original-graph geodesics. Apply the two-geodesic-coverable decomposition theorem.

results.claim: In particular, every outerplanar graph and every planar graph with a universal vertex satisfies the target.
results.proof_sketch: An outerplane graph can be augmented to a triangulated polygon. Its bounded triangular faces, indexed by the weak dual tree, give a tree decomposition with three-vertex bags; deleting augmentation edges retains a decomposition. If planar G has a universal vertex v, deleting v from a plane embedding leaves every other vertex incident with one merged face, so G-v is outerplanar. Add v to every bag of a size-three decomposition of G-v, obtaining bags of size at most four.

results.claim: If the largest component of an n-vertex graph has order m<=floor(n/2)+4, then the target holds. Consequently every nonempty graph on at most eight vertices satisfies it.
results.proof_sketch: If m<=floor(n/2), the graph is already balanced. Otherwise let d=m-floor(n/2)<=4 and delete any d vertices from the unique largest component H. Every remaining part of H has order at most m-d=floor(n/2), and all other original components also have at most that order. This is a balanced separator of order at most four. For connected G, d=ceil(n/2), which is at most four when n<=8.

results.claim: The preceding eight-vertex bound is sharp without planarity.
results.proof_sketch: For n>=9, every nontrivial geodesic of K_n is one edge, so the union of two geodesics contains at most four vertices. Its complement is a connected clique of order at least n-4>n/2. Thus K_n is a counterexample in the unrestricted graph class.

results.claim: A connected graph satisfies the target whenever it has a half-balanced five-vertex separator X for which G[X] contains an induced path a-b-c.
results.proof_sketch: Because ac is not an edge, a-b-c is a shortest a-c path. Join the two remaining vertices of X by any shortest path. These two geodesics cover X, and monotonicity gives balance.

results.claim: A half-balanced isometric cycle is sufficient, regardless of its length.
results.proof_sketch: Partition the cyclic ordering into two contiguous blocks whose sizes differ by at most one. Each corresponding cycle arc has length at most floor(|C|/2). On an isometric cycle every such arc is a shortest path in G. The two arcs cover V(C), so deleting their union is balanced.

results.claim: In a planar graph, the vertex set of every half-balanced 5-cycle is coverable by two geodesics. A half-balanced induced cycle of length six is also coverable in any graph.
results.proof_sketch: On a 5-cycle, if every consecutive two-edge arc had adjacent endpoints, the five cycle edges and five resulting chords would form K_5, impossible in a planar graph. Thus some consecutive triple is a geodesic; the two remaining cycle vertices are adjacent and form the second geodesic. For an induced 6-cycle, split its vertices into two consecutive triples. Each triple is a two-edge geodesic because its endpoints are nonadjacent.

results.claim: A balanced union of three specified geodesics need not have a balanced two-member subunion, even in a planar graph.
results.proof_sketch: For m>=3, start with the 6-cycle a-x-b-y-c-z-a. Attach m-1 leaves to each of a,b,c and one additional pendant leaf x',y',z' to x,y,z. Let P_x=xx', P_y=yy', P_z=zz'. The graph has n=3m+6. Deleting all three paths leaves three components of order m. Deleting, say, P_x and P_y leaves a component consisting of the a- and c-stars together with z,z', of order 2m+2>(3m+6)/2; symmetry handles the other pairs. Nevertheless, two pendant edges at a and b delete their anchors and leave largest component m+4<=(3m+6)/2, so this is only an obstruction to thinning the prescribed triple.

results.claim: There is an explicit 12-vertex planar graph I of diameter three that remains connected after deletion of any four vertices.
results.proof_sketch: Let I have poles N,S, upper vertices u_i, lower vertices l_i (i modulo 5), and edges Nu_i, Sl_i, u_i u_{i+1}, l_i l_{i+1}, u_i l_i, u_i l_{i-1}. The twenty triangles Nu_i u_{i+1}, Sl_i l_{i+1}, u_i u_{i+1}l_i, and u_i l_{i-1}l_i give a sphere embedding. Exact BFS gives diameter three. The persisted checker tested all sum_{j=0}^4 binom(12,j)=794 deletion sets and found the remaining graph connected in every case.

results.claim: The planar graph I has no half-balanced separator formed by one geodesic.
results.proof_sketch: Diameter three implies that a geodesic has at most four vertices. By the preceding four-deletion property, deleting it leaves one connected component of at least 12-4=8 vertices, exceeding |I|/2=6. The exact checker independently rejected all 162 distinct geodesic vertex sets.

results.claim: Two geodesics do half-balance I, so the preceding result establishes genuine necessity of the second path rather than a counterexample to the target.
results.proof_sketch: The paths P_1=u_3-N-u_0-l_0 and P_2=u_3-u_2-u_1-l_0 both have length three. The endpoints u_3,l_0 are nonadjacent and have disjoint neighborhoods, so their distance is three and both paths are geodesics. Their union deletes N,u_0,u_1,u_2,u_3,l_0. The six remaining vertices u_4,l_1,l_2,l_3,l_4,S induce one connected component, exactly meeting the half-balance bound.
